utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are now in open session of this matter. This is the final pretrial conference. For about, I suppose, an hour and a half considered in a closed session the protective measures that needed to be discussed in the closed session. We are now, however, in the open session in the final pretrial conference. I suppose, for the record, we are having this final pretrial conference in temporary quarters, so to speak. The courtroom has been constructed but there is some wiring that is going on. So of course we will begin on Tuesday in the courtroom and we are just here today to conduct the final pretrial conference. Let me reiterate the rulings that have been made on outstanding motions. As I indicated, we are required to issue the decisions in both English and French, but for the benefit of parties I want you to know how we have ruled, first, on the motion for severance of the Defence. That has been denied. The Defence motion regarding contamination of witnesses, that has been denied. There was also a request for an amicus by Courtroom TV, that has been denied as well. Those orders and decisions are in the process of being translated into French and will be issued today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the court pleases, I want to make a very short statement on that. That is, the Defence is quite confused that you disposed of the motions on severance and contamination without having the opportunity to put forward oral arguments. Would it be the case that the Defence will have to ask each time again if we file a motion that we want oral arguments, so we have to file an explicit request ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- for oral arguments, otherwise we have this confusion again?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There should not be any confusion. We had determined in the very beginning of our proceedings, and we have had several status conferences in closed sessions, where we have determined there would not be oral argument absent a request, one, by the movant and then of course a decision by the Trial Chamber to allow oral argument. So we have disposed of any number of motions without oral argument because it has not been requested. Even if it is requested, however, the Chamber again would have to make a determination as to whether we would grant it. That is how we have been operating and we have treated these last motions no differently. Now, the first order of business of the open session will be the motion of the Prosecutor to withdraw counts 2 through 4. That motion as well as the next motion that we will hear from the Defence on we indicated in the scheduling order that we wished to hear oral argument on. So, please will you discuss your motion to withdraw counts 2 through 4, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Having regard to the response filed by the Defence in relation to this particular motion, we ascertained that the only issues that are outstanding are whether or not the withdrawal of counts 2 through 4 is to be done pursuant to Rule 51; whether or not there is to be some limitation in the future on the Prosecutor in ever bringing those counts again before the court, and whether or not the accused can subsequently be arrested and kept in detention on the basis of the counts that we seek to withdraw. Your Honours, firstly, dealing with the question of Rule 51, the Prosecution considers that this is more in the nature of withdrawal of an indictment under Rule 51 than it is an amendment to the indictment. True it is that the indictment will be drawn only in part and will continue on, and the part that is not withdrawn will continue on through the course of the trial. In our submission, Rule 51 is the appropriate Rule to apply for the purposes of withdrawal. We would urge the Chamber to interpret the provisions of withdrawal of the indictment to include by way of interpretation the whole as well as the part. Your Honours, sometimes in statutes of interpretation that we are all accustomed to seeing, we see such a provision, that when reading a piece of legislation the whole is to include the part. We would urge that interpretation on the Chamber, there being no other provision we can see in the Rules which are appropriate having regard to the fact that we consider that this is not an amendment but in fact a withdrawal. Your Honours, dealing then with the question of whether or not there should be some time limit on whether or not the prosecution can commence again -- in particular this is referred to by way of an observation of the Defence, them not objecting to Prosecutor's motion as such, but saying under paragraph 11.2 that at a certain point in time the accused should know whether or not he still faces charges -- your Honours, there is no provision in the Statute or anywhere else to limit the prosecution in bringing charges. In other words, there is no statute of limitation as such on these types of offences. We would argue, your Honours, that it would be not only difficult to create what is, in effect, a statute of limitation on the prosecution, but it may well be beyond the power of the Chamber to do so, having regard to the absence of such a provision in either the Statute or the Rules. In our submission, this is in some jurisdictions dealt with on the basis of a pure common law dealing with the matter, by the court saying that the prosecutor is being unreasonable after the extensive length and the period of time in bringing these charges to proceed with the prosecution and, in particular, having regard to the fact that the accused is being convicted, should that be the case. In those circumstances, what happens in those jurisdictions is that the court simply refuses to lend its jurisdiction to the hearing on the basis that the prosecution is unreasonably bringing the prosecution at such a late stage, or having regard to the fact that the person has previously been prosecuted and there is, in fact, a stay of proceedings sorted. In our submission, that would be an appropriate remedy available to the accused should the prosecution do that at such a time that it is considered to be unreasonable. In our submission, this would afford the accused adequate protection in those circumstances and is certainly preferable to the Chamber having to craft somewhat is, in effect, a statute of limitation. Your Honours, with respect to the final matter, that is the question of subsequent arrest based on the withdrawn counts, our submission to that is that once the counts are withdrawn, then that is the end of the matter; the Prosecutor cannot arrest on those counts because they no longer exist, they have been withdrawn. So there is no basis for the Prosecutor to do that. So, in our submission, that is not a problem that should arise. That is a matter that was raised in paragraph 11.3. Unless there is any other matter that I can assist the Chamber with, they are our submissions in relation to the response of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about the question of whether this motion should be presented to the Trial Chamber or to the confirming judge? Both Rules 50 that governs an amendment of indictment and 51 which governs withdrawal of indictment provide that they will be presented to the judge who confirmed it, but if at trial then the motion would be presented to the Trial Chamber? Are we at trial I suppose, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is perhaps a matter which may ultimately be decided in another place, but as far as our submissions are concerned at this stage, we are on the eve of the trial, motions have been dealt with by this Chamber, and we are so far into the Chamber that, in our submission, we must be at the stage where it could be said that we are trial, with the leave of the Chamber, and would seek leave of this Chamber to dispose of it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence who will present the response to this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I would like to comment shortly, because you have seen already in our response to the motion that we do not basically oppose against the request of the Prosecutor. The matter whether this motion falls within the scope of Article 50 or 51 is not that important for us that I will spend any more time on that. The matter of competence, of course, is a different issue. First of all, I think it would be very a bad start of this Tribunal if organs of the Tribunal, in this case the Trial Chamber, would hear a motion or decide upon a motion of which it is not competent to decide upon. The Defence noticed that on earlier motions that should have been addressed to the confirming judge have also been referred to that confirming judge. So, the Defence would rather stick to a strict keeping to the competence provisions as we find them in the Statute. Then on the merits of the motion itself, the Prosecutor has argued there is no provision dealing with the issue of how long a trial could take, and that is the response to our observation that of course we reserve the right to invoke the violation of the undue delay provision as it is in the Statute. That is also our primary answer, that there is a provision. The provision is in Article 21 of the Statute saying that the accused is entitled to be tried without undue delay. If we look at the case law of the European Court of Human Rights we see that whether a trial is without undue delay is usually decided upon by looking at the whole of the procedure as well as to the specific stages of it. Therefore, I would say that since this case has been referred to the Tribunal after it was already in the hands the German authorities, that this first stage, these first 14 months of detention already in Germany, should be taken into consideration as well if finally a decision would have to be taken on the question of whether there is any undue delay or not. I am not asking your Trial Chamber or the confirming judge to say, well, three years and 10 days, that is the absolute limit, but there is a provision for that that has to be interpreted. As you see, the Defence has drawn your attention to the consequences of the position taken by the Prosecution as far as this motion is concerned. What the Prosecution says as a matter of fact is that if a witness is not available to us, then there could be no fair decision taken in the case. You will understand that this is a very important motion and the Defence is very happy to support this view as strongly as possible. We are aware as well that usually if you have no evidence at the moment the trial starts this would result in an acquittal, but the Prosecution asks for withdrawal without prejudice, this means make the counts sleeping, and I will come to that later because the Prosecution says that in a later stage of course since the counts have been withdrawn there can never be a basis for detention. I do understand that if you ask for withdrawal without prejudice, and I am talking about a sleeping case, there will be an opportunity sooner or later to awake the case again and then, of course, it is not withdrawn any more and it could be the basis for detention as well. So the Defence supports the underlying idea heavily, but at the same time points at all the complications that might result from it. The Prosecution has admitted that at some stage there might be a situation where statute of limitation has been completed. I think that is mixing up two totally different things. The statute of limitation is at least in my idea, but I do not know whether it is different in other systems, a totally different issue compared to the avoiding of undue delay during trial. So, I think that the statute of limitation, as the French call it "description", means you lose your right to prosecute after a certain period of time, a period of time that is usually far longer than what we are talking about here. We are discussing here that the accused is entitled to have a trial without undue delay. If the delay becomes too long, and as I told you in my opinion also the German procedure has to be taken into consideration, then it is not a matter of statute of limitation; it is not a matter of "description" because that starts on from the moment the offence has been committed. Undue delay provisions usually relate to the starting of the proceedings and the time the proceedings take. So I would say that if finally there would be an undue delay, this has nothing to do with statute of limitation, but exclusively with the provision of Article 21 sub (4) (c) of the Statute. I reacted already on the detention. It could never be based upon a withdrawn indictment. I do understand that if it is withdrawn without prejudice that it can be reanimated at a later stage. So I do not think the argument is valid, because I cannot imagine that the Prosecutor once he reanimated the withdrawn counts then would refrain from using whatever powers he would have under the Statute or under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So that is one of the issues. It is only acceptable for the Defence to withdraw, partially withdraw, these counts if this were later not cause to create a new basis for detention. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that under no circumstances then should the Prosecutor be allowed to withdraw the indictment without prejudice, that is must always be with prejudice?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think our response was ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that. It really relates to what you have just said. Your response is you have no objection to the Prosecutor withdrawing or amending the indictment whether it falls within 50 or 51 without prejudice, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We do not oppose against withdrawal without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Without prejudice, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But we think in a later that if the case would be reanimated or awakened, that you could not use these counts again for new detention decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But that would be a matter that would be presented at such a time, if at all, the Prosecutor determines to issue a new indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not something we need to determine at this point, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. The Prosecution asks you not just to give leave for withdrawal, but give a certain interpretation to it. If they are asking for that, I would like to know the consequences of that interpretation for the later stages of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. You have no problem with either 50 or 51, whether it is an amendment or a withdrawal. You do though suggest, or take the position, that the motion should be referred to the confirming judge. You have indicated that that has happened in the past. In this case, and you are correct, when the Prosecutor amended its indictment the first time in the fall of last year, that amendment at least this Trial Chamber asked that it be referred to the confirming judge for consideration and he did and granted the amendment. However, the Prosecutor says that we are further now into the proceeding, that that was in the fall of last year. Now here we are, the eve before trial. Is it your position, I gather from reading your written submission, that this Chamber does have permission to rule on the motion if it is done in trial? If we act in trial, do we have the competence to rule on the motion to amend or withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that is of course a situation that has not been provided for in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, because the motion has been filed prior to trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What you have said your position is that the Trial Chamber could delay ruling on this motion until such a time as the trial begins. My question is, when do you believe the trial begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would not mind that, but one of the things I am fearing as a matter of fact is the consequences of taking this decision after the trial has started, because it is the Prosecution that asked for withdrawal without prejudice. As I indicated, there is no non-bis-in-idem rule for the Tribunal itself. It is very remarkable that there is no provision for that because in all domestic, civilised systems, you find a rule that a court could not try for a second time the same case. Of course then you come to the question that has been discussed before; when a trial has started and we then discussed arraignment under US law. It is quite unclear for me what the consequences will be if the withdrawal will become effective only after the trial has started.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When does trial start in your definition?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: On 7th May, we were informed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, fine. The trial will start on 7th May. Suppose we then grant leave to the Prosecutor on 7th May, either before or after it presents its opening statements, to submit its motion to withdraw? In your judgment, would the Trial Chamber have competence at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think once -- well, a new problem arises. I mean, if it is on 7th May -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us answer the first, would we have competence, and then, of course, we have to deal with the question of whether it should be with or without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have not given it a lot of thought, but I would say that after the opening statements the trial has started, but it is difficult. I am more worried about the consequences of a decision after the trial has started or when a decision has been taken at the pretrial stage. I mean, where it exactly starts is a different thing. I think we have to stick to the rules of the competence. So if the trial has not started yet, it is the confirming judge. I think we should not start with competence to be given to other organs as defined under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and once trial has started, at whatever time that may be on 7th May, at 10 o'clock or 12 o'clock or after opening statement or prior to opening statement, I think I am fearing the consequences of that decision.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that, but let us see if we can resolve one question at a time. It is your position -- this is the position you take in your papers -- that, of course, this Chamber would have competence to rule on the motion once trial starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I ask you then, in your opinion, when does trial start; you say May 7th. That is a good answer. What I am then asking you is whether, if this Chamber then rules on the motion after the opening statements or even before the opening statements, would that be during trial, so that whether we proceed under Rule 50 or 51 this Chamber would have competence to rule on the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just consult. The mere fact that a motion has been filed prior to a trial will not, in the view of the Defence, influence the competence of the Trial Chamber if a decision will be taken on the motion after the beginning of trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your opinion, the trial would begin on May 7th either or before or after opening statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if I stay on the safe side, I would say after the opening statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like that. I think that is, perhaps, more appropriate. Judge Stephen had a question, though, he wanted to present to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me to make one additional remark to that? You will be aware that the opening statement will be influenced by whether these counts are still in it or not, so that is one of the problems if you would decide after the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I am trying to do is to get you to tell us when we would have competence to rule on this motion. Whether it is under 50 or 51, you have said after trial begins and now you have said, of course, after opening statements, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I said that is the safe side. The Defence would not mind to take a less safe position and to do it prior to the opening statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, prior to opening statements. Of course, now I understand that then implicates another question that you have, and that has to do with whether it should be allowed without prejudice which we will get to in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I was merely going to ask you this. Assume that this is done simply by way of an amendment and done at the beginning of the trial on 7th May, can we not leave the whole question of the consequences to the event, if it should ever in the future occur, of new charges dealing with counts 2 to 4 then being raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do agree that we do not ask for a decision on these issues, but we wanted to draw the attention to all the complications that might result from withdrawing these counts of the indictment after the trial has started, but I do not think that we can take a decision now, apart from the detention issue because that is something totally different. But whether the Prosecution could reanimate these counts 2 through 4 again in the near future or in any further future and whether they still were entitled to prosecute these charges at a later stage, I do not think we can decide that now. But since I thought it was of some importance whether this decision was taken prior to trial or during trial, I thought it wise to point out some of these consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we treat this as a motion to amend the indictment, then need we even make a ruling as to whether it is with or without prejudice because you are not withdrawing a portion of the indictment, you are amending an indictment? That is really Judge Stephen's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You will understand that if the consequences would be the same, I mean, an amendment of the indictment, I focused on the wording in French, as a matter of fact, which seems to relate to the document rather than to the contents of it, but of course if the amendment would be that some counts are not prosecuted any more, are withdrawn as a matter of fact off this indictment, then of course it should have the same consequences, whatever they may be, as a withdrawal under the other Article.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regardless of whether you call it an amendment or withdrawal or whether under 50 or 51, your position is that it is treated the same way and we would have to then consider the question of whether it should be with or without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your submission, your written submission, I read it to mean that this is a matter that should be raised at a later time if the Prosecutor ever decides to reindict as to counts 2 through 4, and that is this matter of undue delay is something that would have to be raised at a later proceeding. There is nothing for this Trial Chamber to do with respect to that issue, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is correct. I reacted on the observations of the Prosecution that there was no provision dealing with the issue. I said there was, but that will be an issue that would have to be dealt with under the future prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With respect to with prejudice or without prejudice, as I understand from your written submission, you did not oppose the Prosecutor withdrawing without prejudice. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is still our position.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If that motion is submitted then on Tuesday, May 7th, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, thank you. Is there anything else from the Prosecution on this motion to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I may be able to make some observations about whether or not it is appropriate to do it now or later, but if your Honours are content do it on Tuesday, then rather than go over it now I will leave it until then, but it seems to me that we are at trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that. We will take it, of course, under advisement, but since it is the position of the Defence that we are not, that it would have to be referred to the confirming judge, but since the Defence does not oppose it being presented on May 7th before opening statements, and then it clearly would be a trial ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- it seems to me the more prudent approach is to handle it that way, and then they do not also object to it being submitted without prejudice, but they do want to be granted leave to raise this issue of undue delay should you choose to prosecute in the future. It seems to me that we are closer together now in resolving this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will then take it under advisement and issue a decision probably some time today. The next motion that we wanted to hear oral argument about relates to the Defence's motion for summons and safe conduct and video conference of witnesses. We considered in closed session that portion of the motion dealing with protective measures, but I would like to hear from the Defence, and we indicated in the scheduling order that we wanted to hear oral argument on this motion, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, we would like to make several points with regard to our motion on summons and other protective measures for the Defence witnesses. First of all, I want to repeat and to stress that all these motions, the motions concerning the Defence witnesses, there was a general motion concerned with the video conference, together with a trial brief on the elements of the offences deal with issues fundamental for the presentation of the case by the Defence. The motion referring to the Defence witnesses is, in the opinion the Defence, conditio sine qua non. Without the requested release, the Defence will not be able to present its case properly. Of course, you will understand "properly" in this context means to be able to obtain the attendance and the examination of all witnesses whose appearances are necessary for an effective defence. It seems that already on these issues the Prosecution and the Defence take different positions. At least from the Prosecution's response to the motion on summons and protections, it appears that the Prosecution is led by the idea that "the accused is entitled to a fair trial, not a perfect trial at which the accused has every witness he requests", page 5 of the response. The Defence takes the position that the right of the accused to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf should not be limited unless the rare, unheard of case that the accused wishes to filibuster a trial which, I would say, is not the case here. I submit that it is for the Defence to decide how to present its case and not for others to curtail the list of witnesses. May this be true in general, in this case we carefully have selected our witnesses on the basis of necessity and availability. That last criterion, the availability of witnesses, has been a major problem for the Defence, together with locating and having access to witnesses. We have told you about that at the previous sessions. That kind of problems causes most of our problems. The Defence has certainly not been fooling around, nor have we presented extreme wishes to the court. As contrast to the 120 witnesses we have been given notice by the Prosecution to be called by the Prosecution, the Defence has so far given notice of about 36 witnesses. As a matter of fact, we are only led by the concept of securing proper defence of our client against the charges. To present our case, it is essential to take appropriate measures to make the evidence of our witnesses available to the court. That is our main concern. Now let me run through the various aspects of the motion. First, I am going to deal with the exceptional circumstances. It seems to the Defence that it can hardly be contested that this Tribunal functions under extremely exceptional circumstances, as long as the circumstances in Bosnia have not normalised. We are dealing here with an integrated area where fear from persons in power, corrupted relations and failing public safety frustrate a normal execution of justice, while on top of this a co-operation with the Tribunal is not secured. I note that the Prosecution did not contest that we are dealing here with these kinds of extraordinary situations. Since we discussed extensively the specific circumstances that the Tribunal is not a judicial body functioning in the context of a State and its organs and legal instruments in June last year, I think it would not be necessary to elaborate on that issue again. So I take it that the court will accept that the Defence has correctly asserted in paragraph 1 of the motion of summons and protection that we are dealing here with exceptional circumstances, exceptional reasons, exceptional measures. That brings me to the issue of the second paragraph dealing with the request for summons or subpoenas.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question regarding the first paragraph? I do not want you to think that we have accepted with certainty the allegations that you have made in paragraph 1, exceptional circumstances, because, for example, you say that the authorities of Republika Srpska do not formally recognise the Tribunal or, at least, refuse to co-operate with the Tribunal. The Dayton Accords now certainly require co-operation. I do not know that is something this Tribunal can accept, that they will not co-operate with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not asking the Tribunal to accept non-co-operation; I am just telling you that the reality is they are not accepting the co-operation. It may be a part of the Dayton Agreement, but being an effective agreement, that is a different question. I am just arguing here that being it in formal terms a provision of the Dayton Agreement that the Serbian Republic will have to co-operate, and being it your position that they will have to co-operate also on the basis of Article 28 of the Statute, the reality is that they do not. We are conducting this trial under the reality that witnesses are living in that area dealing with authorities who, in effect, do not co-operate and, therefore, are hindering the witnesses to do as they please. So witnesses here are requested by the Defence to come forward and to talk to us and to be available here in The Hague and, as a matter of fact, they do only what is good for them under the reality of that area, whatever the legal position of the Tribunal may be or whatever the legal implications of the Dayton Agreement may be. So we should not be deal with the matter in theoretical terms, but we have to deal with the matter as practice, daily practice, learns as what reality is, otherwise we are here, I think, conducting a trial that has nothing to do with reality. The reality is that they have to deal with authorities that do not co-operate, that do not, in fact, recognise the Tribunal; I wish they did otherwise but they do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Earlier we talked about having video conferencing -- I am sure you will address this -- in Banja Luka. That, of course, is in the Republic of Srpske. We talked about whether or not that was even realistic considering the attitude that has been taken by the Republic. It seems to me that if that is the case, then when we get to video conferencing it is really going to be just pie in the sky; if they are not co-operating, why should we even talk about it? I hope that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is a difference between, let us say, co-operating and not opposing it. Let me give you an example. The mass graves that have been under investigation now, we have seen that though there is not a co-operation of the authorities over there, as a matter of fact, they do not oppose the officials of the Tribunal being there under cover of IFOR. That is exactly what we are going to deal with here. If the Tribunal decides to grant a video link testimony, then I would say that we have no indication that the authorities over there will oppose that. I take it that the Tribunal will be able, just as has been the case with those mass graves, that under cover of IFOR you will be able to establish a video link provision over there. Your position, as the Tribunal -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They will not co-operate then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They will not co-operate; they will just do nothing; they will abstain. We are not dealing here with anything the Tribunal will do, if I am talking about the witnesses; we are talking here about individuals with no authority and they have a different position to those authorities than the Tribunal has, because the Tribunal may experience that the authority abstain but the witnesses do not experience such an abstention. They have to deal with the authorities dealing with them. So that is the extraordinary circumstance here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is prepared to summons the 23 witnesses. I think you have asked for 23 witnesses to be summonsed ought of the 28 you have listed, and we are prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. I will not address that any more. As far as the safe conduct is concerned, Mr. Orie will put forward oral arguments on that issue; maybe he can do it after me and I will continue with the video link, if you please. Before discussing the request for video link testimony, the Defence joins the Prosecution in its request for the application of Rule 4, that is, that the Trial Chamber will exercise its functions partly on location. That might be the case not in Prijedor, as suggested by the Prosecution, because then I think we are looking for trouble, but that will not be a problem as far as I judge the situation in Banja Luka. Partly conduct of the trial on location where the witnesses are available will certainly benefit the presentation of the case. The Defence have no doubt about that. In its response, page 5, the Prosecution makes a formal request to the Trial Chamber to enter such an order, and if such an order will be endorsed, the Defence will abstain from its request No. 2.1 to grant the Defence witness to testify by video link. But if the Trial Chamber will not conduct a part of the trial on location, the Defence asserts that the witnesses as listed under request 2.1 should be allowed to testify by video link. I will go into that matter. The basis for this request is not primarily found in Rule 71, but in Rule 90(A) in connection with Rule 71(D). In the system of the Rules, as we see it, the provision of Rule 71 does not only function in the context of pretrial proceedings but also in the context of proceedings before the Trial Chamber. In our opinion, the scope of paragraph (A) of Rule 90 is to enable the availability of witnesses' evidence during the trial, not only by means of a classical disposition of a witness before the beginning of the trial, but also during the trial by modern means of communication. It seems consistent with the reference in paragraph (A) of Rule 90 that the means of video conference of paragraph (D) of Rule 71 is not only designed to provide for an alternative of (indecipherable) a witness, but also for a video link giving of evidence during the trial itself. This interpretation of Rule 90 and Rule 71 fits perfectly well into the specific circumstances of the up-coming trial. We are dealing here, are we not, with witnesses that could have been deposed prior to the trial if the Prosecution had access to the area, and if the Prosecution had been able to be present during the Defence interviews of the witnesses. We know that efforts of the Defence to achieve that have not been successful, and that is not due to any matter we are responsible for. If such a deposition could have taken place, though it did not take place for reasons beyond the responsibility of the Defence, I do not see any reason why the same provision of Rule 71(D), though in the context of Rule 90(A), could not be used in a later stage during the trial when possible. So the application of Rule 71(D) in the context of Rule 90(A) means that the trial may proceed uninterrupted while limited interpretation of these Rules would implicate a postponement of the trial in order to enable a deposition solely under Rule 71. Where the Trial Chamber will have to ensure the expeditious trial -- Article 20 of the Statute -- the Defence suggests that Rules 90 and 71 should be understood to enable a request for giving evidence by video link. That being the case, the Prosecution contested that the Defence did not make a sufficient showing to justify the measures, so what is then the standard here for such a justification? The Defence asserts that, consistent to the interpretation of Rule 71 by the judges in the first annual report, the fact that the witness is not willing to testify in The Hague is enough. The Prosecution has not contested that the witnesses are not willing to testify in The Hague. It only has suggested that the Defence will sufficiently have to show why the witness is not willing to testify in The Hague. This issue of "why" seems not to be the standard here. The Defence has provided affidavits to establish the fact that the witnesses are not willing to testify in The Hague. That is enough, but even if the standard would be different, the Defence have provided the court with affidavits to establish that under the extraordinary circumstances of the witnesses, it is subjectively not unreasonable of the witness not to be willing to testify in The Hague, being the issue of unwilling and subjective interpretation of the witness of his own position, there is no room for an objective standard. The second issue raised by the Prosecution is that the Defence did not disclose the matters upon which the witness will testify. To the opinion of the Defence, a notice of alibi sufficiently discloses that all the witnesses will testify about the whereabouts of the accused at times as described in the indictment. Since the indictment is vague about these dates, notification is confined to the same parameters of non-precision. It seems highly unfair to the Defence to ask for more details when the Prosecution fails to supply such details to the Defence. The information about matters upon which the witnesses will testify, if granted giving evidence by video link, is sufficient to the standard of Rule 71(B) in connection with rules 67 (A)(i) from which it follows in this case that the Defence has no obligation to disclose more than as described in subsection A of section (ii) of paragraph (A) of Rule 67. Being it in the interests of justice that the Defence will be able to make available to the court evidence to be given by video link, I have no doubt that your Trial Chamber will accept that the requirements of Rule 71 in connection with Rule 90 have been met by the Defence. If the Trial Chamber will rule as requested, it seems not necessary to grant the request of the Prosecution to have a trial attorney present on location. Such a presence will reduce the advantage of a video link testimony to zero; whereas the witness will fear that the Prosecutor present will use its powers to make arrests. The Defence suggests that an officer of the Registry will be present to determine that the witness is who he or she purports to be. The presence of such a presiding officer would also be preferable in the case of an anonymous witness. Those are the remarks I wanted to make about the motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who will respond for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May we deal also with safe conduct before the Prosecution so we have the whole matter?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us talk about video link if we can, separate that, hear the Prosecution and then we will come back, please.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the Prosecution noted in its response to the Defence motion, we do not in principle have a blanket opposition to video link testimony. We do not believe it falls under Rule 71. We do not believe the Defence is asking for deposition. In fact, they are asking for live testimony during the trial by means of video link. We believe that it is within the authority of this court to order that. So we have no blanket opposition to it in principle. We do oppose the Defence application for this relief because we do not believe they have made a sufficient showing. Listening to the Defence argument on this requested relief, the Prosecution notes basically two premises. The first is that the Defence never has any obligation to make any showing because they are the Defence, they are representing the accused, so they may simply ask for something, give a conclusion as to how important it is to them and that must be granted. We do not believe that is what the Rules or the Statute envisions, nor do we believe that is what a fair trial requires. Secondly, we now understand that the Defence believes that in addition to having these witnesses testify by void link from a separate location far removed from here, they also believe that somehow they have a right inherent in this request to preclude the Prosecution from being present should the Prosecution elect to be present with the witnesses and to physically confront the witness and to physically question the witness at that location. We do not believe there is any basis in the Rules for that nor in the Statute. Hence, they would ask you not only to grant the video link request but to specifically preclude the Prosecution from having someone present at this distant location to question this witness in person. First of all, let us examine the premise that the Defence has no obligation to make any showing in this case. It may be true, even with some limitations there, that if the Defence is presenting evidence and witnesses in the normal course of the proceedings as the proceedings envision that evidence to be presented, then of course they have wide latitude to decide what their case requires and to present evidence to support their case. Even there we suggest there are limitations such as relevance, unduly collateral matters being introduced into the proceedings. There are various balancing factors that the court may use to even at that point say that the Defence may not present evidence. However, when (as here) the Defence wants particular relief that is contrary to the normal course of proceedings, then we suggest, yes, indeed, the Defence has a burden to make a sufficient showing to allow those particular measures of relief to be granted to them. One of the showings they must make is that, in fact, this witness is important enough to these proceedings to determining the truth of these proceedings and important enough to the Defence that this court should deviate from the normal procedure and allow this specific relief. In this instance, the normal procedure is that, as the Rule states, in principle, witnesses will be heard in person before the Trial Chamber. That, I believe, the Rule means physically present before the Trial Chamber. So they are asking for relief from the normal procedure. They have not supported their request for that relief. It could be that if a witness is sufficiently important and will not come here, then of course video link testimony maybe the only way to ensure the accused a fair trial, but you cannot make that determination until you know at least the essence of what this witness will testify to. The Defence says the Prosecution here, by making this requirement or trying to place this requirement on the Defence, is actually asking the Defence to give more detail than the Prosecution has given. By making that assertion, however, the Defence is ignoring a very substantial fact. We have not given the Defence only the indictment. We have given the Defence statements or offers of proof concerning every one of the witnesses we intend to call. Those statements or offers of proof talk about where the witness was when he or she experienced what they experienced; they talk about a general time frame; they talk in many instances about a time of day or night; they talk about the circumstances in which they found themselves; they present the Defence with a great deal of evidence to assist them in determining if they are going to present an alibi what are the relevant times, what is the relevant alibi they have to present. In determining if they should be allowed an extraordinary measure to present a purported alibi witness, then we suggest that they should present to the court and to the Prosecution (so we may challenge it if we feel appropriate) the general testimony that witness will give. Where does the witness say they were with this accused, during what time frame, at what time of the day or night? Those are matters that are very significant to this Trial Chamber in determining if this particular relief to do something outside the normal proceedings is, in fact, required to afford the accused a fair trial. They have not made such a showing. Should they make such a showing, we believe it is within the power of the Trial Chamber to order video link testimony. We believe, however, the order would have to include language and requirements such that these witnesses, wherever they are testifying, would be testifying in such a setting that the integrity of these proceedings could be protected; that is, they would be testifying in some type of setting that would be akin to this courtroom, conducive to truth telling and, of course, to them being who they say they are, conducive to no outside influences directing their testimony in a courtroom. So we again, in principle, do not oppose this idea of video link testimony but, in practicality, we believe that the Defence definitely does have a burden, that a balancing test that you must make in this case requires they meet that burden and provide much more detail than they have. For that reason we would ask at this time that you deny this request.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, let me see if I can just put this in the framework that we see, at least as judges, having reviewed the motion and the response. You have provided a list of 28 witnesses, Mr. Wladimiroff, as I understand it ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- that are the subject of this motion, different relief for different ones, 28 witnesses. All of these witnesses are listed as alibi witnesses; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of the 28 now, 14 you want to offer testimony by via the video link, according to our calculations. There are two rules then that the parties suggest address depositions. (1), Mr. Wladimiroff, you mentioned Rule 90(A) that provides the witnesses shall, in principle, be heard directly by the Chambers unless a Chamber has ordered that the witness be heard by means of a deposition as provided for in Rule 71. Then 71(D) provides that deposition evidence may also be given by means of a video conference. So the first question is whether or not what you are asking for, that is, the testimony of these 14 witnesses, is truly a deposition or is it some kind of testimony at a location other than the court in the courtroom here in The Hague? It appears that it may not be a deposition necessarily, but something akin to testimony other than at the Hague. The Prosecutor says we have this inherent power to order this even if it is not specifically provided for in the Rule. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is our position indeed, because we feel that Article 90 at paragraph (A) is dealing with your powers during the trial. You may solve the problem in two ways. As far as 90(A) refers to 71, you may read Rule 71 in the context of a pretrial provision that provides for this posting of a witness being the Prosecution present to cross-examine, and you can do it, let us say, and a presiding officer on the basis of a transcript of what has been done, or by means of a video conference. But you could also read Rule 71 in the context of Rule 90(A) as a provision for the Trial Chamber not to interrupt the trial for deposition, but to use 71 as a means to hear witnesses not being present in the courtroom physically, but being present through the image on the television screen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 71(A) provides that at the request of either party, a Trial Chamber may, in exceptional circumstances and in the interests of justice, order that a deposition be taken for use at trial, and appoint for that purpose a Presiding Officer. It is your position that you should not have to make a showing for the video conference anything different than what is provided for or anything greater than what is provided for in 67(A)(ii)(a), and that refers to the defence of alibi. It just says that the defence shall specify the place or places at which the accused claims to have been present at the time of the alleged crime and the names and addresses of the witnesses and any other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely. What you are saying is you do not have to show anything more, if you want a video conference of alibi witnesses, than what is in this Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I am saying is that under Rule 71 at paragraph (B) there is a requirement of provide for statement of matters on which a person is to be examined. What we are saying here is the notification under Rule 67(A)(ii)(a) provides for that information, and we are not bound to provide more than we are obliged to according to the Rules. Rule 71, paragraph (B), is not a Rule by itself; it is in the context of the whole Rules. We provided sufficient information because we provided the Prosecution with the places and dates where the accused was in the whole period of time of the indictment. We have provided them also with the witnesses who are able to give evidence about those places and dates. What more should we provide them with? There is a dispute. The Chamber will be hearing a motion later because the Prosecution takes the position we have to provide them with copies of our statements of interviews. We take the position we have not. So, here it comes back; we say we have not to provide them any more than we have to provide them under the Rules. So, the understanding of 71, section (B), should be that 71 under (B) may not go beyond the parameters of 67(A)(ii)(a).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the effect of 71(A) that deals with depositions and says that in exceptional circumstances and in the interests of justice the deposition may be ordered? What kind of showing need you make to meet these exceptional circumstances and in the interests of justice requirement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have to make that showing. I am not disputing that. I am taking the position that we have shown that we are dealing here with exceptional circumstances as described in paragraph 1 of the motion. I have added arguments to that now here in this hearing. It is certainly in the interests of justice that the Defence will be able to present its case, to bring evidence which will only be available to the court if the measures are granted. As a matter of fact, we are dealing here with the same argument as has been used by the Prosecution to explain why they are going to withdraw counts 2 to 4, that is, that the fairness of your decision on the case will be affected if not either party is able to bring forward all evidence that is available. What we are arguing here is that it is in the interests of justice, and that should be understood in terms of a fair trial, that the Defence struggling with extreme problems, as I explained before, will be able to present evidence that is essential for the case. It has also been disputed by the Prosecution that we did not show the importance of those witnesses for the case of the Defence. I would say that the importance is self-explanatory because we filed a notification of defence of alibi. A defence of alibi in this case is essential to our case. The case is based on that defence. So for that reason it can hardly be disputed that we just at random bring witnesses to the court because we feel these are the essential witnesses which form the basis of our defence of alibi. So that is in the interests of justice, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is in the interests of justice that you be allowed to offer testimony, that is for sure. Let me ask you a couple of questions though about these 14 witnesses, if I may. No. 9, for example, you ask for testimony to be given through video link.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say that this individual has been detained in a detention camp. You say that the witness is prepared to testify by video link but fears that her testimony may cause her danger in the Bosnian-Serb Republic. Is it your position that that is a sufficient statement of the reasons why in the interests of justice we should allow testimony by video link,, assuming that we have the inherent power and it does not fit within the deposition rules, have you made a sufficient showing for 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We feel we have, because it has become clear that the Defence is dealing with witnesses who live without any exception in the area. If it has become clear that the Defence is dealing with very limited possibilities to locate and to have access to witnesses, and if it has become clear that the Defence may be limited to just a few witnesses who will only testify if the giving of evidence will be granted in the circumstances they feel safe, then not granting such measures will simply result in falling down of the case. We better the rest case the because otherwise we have no witnesses except for, let us say, five and that compared to the 120 witnesses on the side of the Prosecution all living outside the former Yugoslavia, is this specific circumstance in this case brings to light that we are dealing here with extreme circumstances which are not the usual circumstances in domestic courts. So we have to look for a solution that enables the availability of that little evidence that we have gathered to bring forward in court directly or indirectly. I can hardly imagine that the court will simply say, "Well, it is your problem, we are not going to deal with that by measures you have requested for" and then we will just show, present, our case on that, let us say, five witnesses being the problem of the Defence, because you well do know -- I would say it should be recognised -- that the Tribunal has started its work under very difficult circumstances in the area. The Tribunal started the pretrial of Dusko Tadic while the conflict was ongoing. Only since December 15th the situation has changed, but that is not a change that has enabled the Defence to do what a proper Defence should do. So these extreme circumstances, I would say, justify the extreme measures we are asking for. That may not be the case in future cases, but here, being the first case that started under such rare circumstances, we have no other alternative. Without these witnesses, we have no case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With respect to 9, what you have said in your declaration is that the witness is prepared to testify by video link but fears that her testimony may cause her danger in the Bosnian-Serb Republic. My question is whether or not that is a sufficient showing. For No. 22, you say that this witness prefers to be examined by video link. So my question really goes to whether you have shown enough in the declaration. I understand your limitations, but I am really focusing on the declaration because that is what we have to look at and rule upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After the declaration concerning witness 9 has been signed, we have heard about threats to that witness. So far, we may add to the affidavit new information; if necessary, we might file it as an additional affidavit. With respect to witness 22, the reality is that that witness only wishes to come and testify if he can do it on location. The word "preference" should be understood in a very strong sense. It is not a preference, "I would like to be here", it means that he only prefers to be here as a witness if he is heard as a witness on location.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I imagine most people would prefer not to come to The Hague. It is quite a distance. I can understand that he prefers the other one may suffer some injury and you say that there have been some threats. Then 27, is that M?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is N, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then N is the one you have not interviewed. Again, do you feel that you have made a sufficient showing for video link testimony for a witness whom you have not interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, a defence of alibi -- well, let us put it this way. A defence in this case may stand on two feet: One of the defence of alibi in the strict sense of the word, that is, providing for witnesses who will establish an alibi in the sense of the whereabouts of the witnesses and the direct meaning of he was here and he was not there; the second foot of such an defence is that you will have to provide for witnesses who will say, "At least he was not in a specific camp because I was there". That is an indirect way of an alibi, is it not? So, what we have tried to do is to look for witnesses who have been in those camps, being a detainee or being otherwise engaged in that camp. If you are looking for the last class of witnesses, those who have been otherwise engaged -- I am not going to specify that -- in those camps, it is obvious that no-one who has been engaged in one or other way in a camp, not being a detainee, will come to The Hague. All those witnesses so far we have spoken to do say, "We will only testify if we are protected". We did not speak to witness N, that is right, but being in that class there is no doubt that we are well-established if we say that this witness will certainly not come to The Hague and will only testify under the protection that we have asked for. We are aware of essential evidence that this witness may give about the non-presence of our client in the camp he was engaged in. So it is a vital witness for us and we cannot show more than this, and I think it is sufficient under the circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your position regarding the Prosecutor not being present, in a typical deposition in our Rules, speaking in terms of deposition, in 90 and in 71, deposition testimony, of course, opposing counsel is always there and, of course, the accused or a party to the litigation would also have the right to be there. I gather Mr. Tadic would not be at the site where you envision this, but that may be something that you wish to waive, but why do you take the position that the Prosecutor should not be at the site present to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If you see it as a deposition in the strict sense of 71, not in relation to 90(A), then you are right, a member of the Prosecution should be there, but then we would wish them to abstain of any powers to arrest. If you look into the matter as a provision during the trial based on 90(A) in relation to 71 but not as deposition but as a video link giving evidence, then it is not essential for the Prosecution to be there because we are all in a courtroom being able to put forward examination and cross-examination directly. So the only concern would be someone of the Registry to be there to secure the circumstances of giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it is a deposition (and those are the words that are used at least), then, of course, traditionally opposing counsel would be there, but you view this more as a provision that is not really in the Rules but it is something different than a deposition and, therefore, the Prosecution should not be there because they are in court and they may cross-examine from the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is exactly what we are aiming for. We do not read the word "deposition" in the strict sense as it has been used in the context of a pretrial provision. Since it is linked through 98, we read it not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have anything else, Mr. Wladimiroff, regarding this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, unless you are going to deal with the safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor have anything regarding request for video link -- anything further?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we simply want to point out that we have great sympathy for the Defence's positions. In regard to whether they have shown extraordinary circumstances continue to prevail in the area, the Prosecution would be remiss without pointing out the following to the court, that is, that the Prosecution has sent a team into Opstina Prijedor in February and early March of this year. At that time we met with great resistance from the local authorities. We were escorted by IFOR. We refused to leave even though that was very strenuously suggested that is what we should do. Ultimately, there was co-operation to the extent that we were not arrested for being there. However, there was non-co-operation on other matters. So I believe that the Defence is not being unreasonable in saying that the requirements of the Dayton Agreement aside, the practicalities of the situation are that they may very well be facing this lack of co-operation that they say. We want the court to have the benefit of our experience in determining that issue because we are not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are suggesting that the court go there ---

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- to look for some co-operation?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- because we believe you would have protection and we believe, by the way, that would be one way of imposing upon that area the authority of the Agreement and of this Tribunal. That is, perhaps, a philosophical point, but we do not believe that avoiding an area because they do not want us there is a way of showing that we have right to be there. But that is, as I say, a philosophical point aside. A few other points: As far as the language in the motion concerning witness F, the Defence is correct about the language. What they have failed, of course, to mention is that the Defence had a redacted statement of F and statements of other witnesses who may have had some collateral corroboration for F and could review those statements in determining whether they were going to object to us presenting a sufficient basis for our motion. So they had the information. Again, the point here is not that we are in principle opposed to video link testimony; the point is there must be a sufficient showing. The Defence, as well as the Prosecution, must make a sufficient showing; they very simply have not. They have given you conclusions. In order to determine if fairness requires something, if the interests of justice requires something, if the integrity of the proceedings are to be maintained by a certain procedure, it must be an informed choice on your part; not based upon our conclusions about the importance of the witness but at least some understanding of the material about which this witness will testify. So you can determine how relatively important it is. It is the showing that they fail to make; it is not the principle we oppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you this? I do not at all understand why there is some suggestion that somebody from the Prosecution should be present in Republika Srpska if there is to be a video link and should there cross-examine; why can he not do that just as well, if there is to be a video link, by being present in the courtroom here and, of course, communicating by the video link with the person who is giving evidence, as long as there is present somebody from the Registry at the other end to ensure that the person is giving evidence freely and without any duress?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position on this is that the Defence is requesting that they voluntarily will question a witness outside the physical presence of that witness, and they are asking you to voluntarily agree that you will hear the testimony outside the physical presence of the witness. I think everyone in this room would agree that the best approach is to be in the physical presence of witness. What the Prosecution is simply pointing out is that our preference would be to cross-examine them in the physical presence of the witness. Is it possible to effectively cross-examine and be outside their physical presence? Yes, we believe it is, but our preference (and we believe it should be an option we would have) would be to do it in their presence, certainly with someone present to ensure the person is not reading from any notes, that they are who they purport to be, that the protections for the integrity of the Tribunal are met. It certainly could be done that. So it is merely our preference in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have anything else on video link? I think we have a good understanding, but you may supplement, if you want, and then go on to safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Two small things: If the Prosecution will abstain of making arrest while being present at the video link giving evidence, we will not oppose a representative of the Prosecution being present. The main thing is not making arrests, because that is the essential thing we are arguing here. I would say it is not necessary, but if their preference is to be present, then they will have to commit themselves not to make arrests on location. The second issue, I just want to touch on this, if (I hope not) the Trial Chamber might find that any of our showing is not sufficient, we would rather have you tell us, then we may file additional information you may require instead of just denying the motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There are three of the witnesses for whom you want video link, I gather, and you are asking that the Prosecutor not arrest camp guards; is that correct? 26, 27 and 28?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have not referred to camp guards I have said "people who have been engaged".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: "People who have been engaged".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: "In those camps".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are not 26, 27 and 28?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am just looking into the filings. I have said that witness N worked in a detention camp and that is all what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: M worked as well and O worked as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So we did not specify any function whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding safe conduct request, how long, Mr. Orie, do you anticipate that you will need to present this argument? I am told it is 1 o'clock -- actually it is five after one; we should be taking a lunch recess; is that not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Since I have to make some observation on an undefined subject, it might take me approximately 20 minutes to clarify my position.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think, perhaps, for the benefit of the persons who have to do more than listen, then we will stand in recess -- we have to recess until 2.30, is that not so -- until 2.30 and then we will hear from you. (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, I believe that you were going to present an argument regarding the request for safe conduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I first wanted to apologise for being a bit late but some of the logistics here, it takes us a bit more time. I have prepared some comment on the subject of safe conduct, but after what I have heard this morning, I think that it has even a more general meaning, because you could formulate a question that is at stake also in a more general way, and then the question would be: What is the proper solution if a court has no effective means of compelling witnesses to appear in court? That is both through for the safe conduct issue as well as for perhaps the video conference subject we discussed this morning. Such a situation hardly ever exists in a domestic system. The situation does exist wherever the witness is residing in a place where the jurisdiction that wants to hear him as a witness has no effective power to compel him to appear in court. To this extent, we are dealing, as a matter of fact, with a structural exceptional situation. We have discussed this morning about what is exceptional, what is normal, do you have to compare it with the domestic system? We are faced with a situation that is, from a structural point of view, exceptional. Let me go to the issue of the safe conduct and let me first clarify the misunderstanding we might have caused. It was a question of the Prosecution, whether safe conduct was only asked for for witnesses 3, 17, 14 and 20 or also for witnesses M, N and O. It was not our intention to ask for safe conduct for the witnesses M, N and O but, as I told you before, the observations might have some relevance as well for the situation when a decision would be taken that witnesses would be heard by means of a video link. The Prosecution has responded to our motion saying that we introduced an undefined concept, the safe conduct was undefined. Therefore, I first have to clarify that. I must say that I was a bit surprised that it was regarded to be an undefined concept, because if I try to look into those systems where my learned opponents are coming from to see whether it was known over there, and I saw that Mr. Abell in his book "Judicial Assistance" writes that apart from two exceptions all mutual assistance treaties concluded by the United States of America contained a safe conduct clause, so that unknown it might not be. For Europeans article 12 of the European Convention, Mutual Assistance in criminal matters, also contains a similar clause. For those who might come from Australia, Article 14 of the Dutch Australian Treaty on the Mutual Assistance also gives a safe conduct clause. So I was a bit surprised that it was regarded as being undefined, because what exactly does it mean? The safe conduct provisions protect a person from prosecution and restriction of liberty in the requesting country in relation to acts which preceded his departure from the requested company for purposes of appearing and testifying in response to the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, would you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it the definition, more or less, given by Mr. Abell in his book International Judicial Assistance, I think it is part 3, Mutual Assistance. It says: "The safe conduct provisions protect a person from prosecution and restriction of liberty in the requesting country in relation to acts which preceded his departure from the requested country for purposes of appearing and testifying in response to the request". If I take, for example, the wording of Article 12 of the European Convention on Mutual Assistance, it says in Article 12 under (1): "A witness or expert, whatever his nationality, appearing on a summons before the judicial authorities of the requesting party shall not be prosecuted or detained or subjected to any other restriction of his personal liberty in the territory of that party in respect of acts or convictions anterior to his departure from the territory of the requested party". So it is a similar wording you will find and you will find similar wordings in all the treaties that have a safe conduct clause. You even find broader concepts. I will not discuss them. For example, Article 9 of the US Dutch Mutual Assistance treaty of 1981 gives even protection against any civil law suits, but that is not very relevant at this moment. This concept of safe conduct applies independent from whether there is any reason to protect the witness or whether the witness really fears for arrest. If you would look, for example, in recommendation No. R83-12 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, you will see that they suggest that it should be just a routine procedure, once you call a witness and you use the assistance of the requested country, immediately inform that witness that he will have a safe conduct when he appears as a witness. Well, what is the rationale behind this concept of safe conduct? It is not primarily to protect the witness, but it is to encourage witnesses that cannot be compelled to appear in court to follow the call for appearing in court. It mainly serves the principle of the best evidence. It is in the interests of justice to have witnesses to be present at trial rather than to examine them by letters rogatory, by deposition or at a distance by video link. So the protection of the witness is not the important rationale, but it is the quality of the administration of justice. Safe conduct only applies where the witness cannot be compelled to appear. Therefore, there is no need for applying the concept of safe conduct under domestic law. So if I heard this morning that, well, the requests we made are not very normal, it just depends on what is the context in which you regard it as normal or as abnormal. Under domestic law, there never is any reason to grant a safe conduct, because if a witness fears to be arrested, he can be arrested anyhow as long as he is found within the jurisdiction that needs him as a witness, but also is interested to see him as a suspect or even as a sentenced person. The powers that can be exercised under domestic law will have a double effect simultaneously. The witness can be compelled to appear, thus serving the interests of justice -- the interests of justice that no source of information is unavailable to find the truth -- and at the same time the witness will not escape justice in his own case. The Prosecutor, at least if I read his response, is complaining a bit that the Defence is alleging prosecutorial misconduct and abuse of powers. The Defence has observed, on the one hand, that there is a necessity to grant safe conduct in an international context where witnesses cannot be compelled to appear in order to protect the quality of the administration of justice and, on the other hand, the Defence observes the refusal of the Prosecutor to support the granting of a safe conduct for witnesses, even if these witnesses themselves ask for it. We tried to discuss the issue already somewhere last October prior to making suggestions on whether new rules could be adopted on this issue, but we could not come to an agreement with the Prosecutor. So, that is what we observe. The result of the attitude of the Prosecution is the acceptance of a level of fairness or, perhaps, at the end we should say unfairness, a level of fairness that is far below the standards that are applied under all domestic systems known to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, may I just interrupt you a moment? What is it that you wish this Tribunal to order by way of safe conduct. From reviewing your submission, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what it is, what relief you are asking for for these four witnesses? There are four witnesses, as I understand it, out of the 28 that you have listed that you wish safe conduct. What does that mean? What kind of order would you want the Tribunal to enter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
