utterances.text: We would want the Tribunal to give an order similar to the text I cited before, that the Tribunal orders that when these witnesses appear in The Hague that none of the organs of the Tribunal, especially not the Prosecutor's Office -- will protect these witnesses from prosecution at that time, not later on. It is limited in time. If you look at those provisions granting safe conduct, it is not forever, it is just for the time when they are needed as witnesses in the requested country.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then it would be an order directed to the Prosecutor not to arrest any of the four witnesses who you have identified in your motion. It would not be an order directed to countries that the witnesses might travel to get here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will come to that later, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I just did not understand from your paper. Just tell us what you would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We observe that the result of this attitude is an acceptance of a level of fairness that is below the normal standards. The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe acknowledges that the importance of a safe conduct granted to witnesses is the importance in the view of taking the right decision in the criminal case itself. That is the main rationale. So I think they understood quite well that the fairness of the trial was at stake. The Defence does not suggest that the Prosecutor being estopped from carrying out investigations of any persons identified as Defence witnesses, but just that the Prosecutor refrains from any measure involving restrictions of liberty of the witnesses whilst they are in The Hague for the purpose of giving evidence. A safe conduct, therefore, is limited in its effect and in time as well. It does not limit the Prosecution in whatever way to proceed against the witnesses when this witness has returned to his home country, or even when he decides not to return and stay in The Hague after a certain period of time. The Defence wonders why the Prosecutor gave a totally inadequate picture of the consequences of a safe conduct to support its claim that a safe conduct would be antithetical to the interests of justice. When the Prosecutor complains about a lack of a concise definition -- we have to apologise but we thought that these hundreds of provisions would be well known to the Prosecution -- of what a safe conduct exactly means, the Defence gets the impression that the Prosecutor prefers not to know what a safe conduct in hundreds of multi-lateral treaties implicates in the international relations between states. This impression that the Prosecutor seems not even to want to know what it is became even stronger when we read some of the questions they put to the Defence. We are highly surprised by the Prosecutor's questions of what it would mean, for example, for the government of the Netherlands -- and quote -- "should they be prohibited from pursuing its own domestic interest with respect to persons it suspects of committing" I think they meant of having committed, " ... having committed crimes against humanity". That is the question. The answer to the question is clearly, yes, that is what it means. We do not understand, as a matter of fact, why it is a question, because if I read Article 18 of the Agreement between the United Nations and the Kingdom of the Netherlands concerning the headquarters of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia it says: "Without prejudice to the obligations of host country to comply with a request for assistance made or orders issued by the Tribunal pursuant to Article 29 of its Statute, witnesses and experts appearing from outside the host country on a summons or a request of the Tribunal or the Prosecutor shall not be prosecuted or detained or subjected to any other restriction of their liberty by the authorities of the host country in respect of acts or convictions prior to their entry into the territory of the host country". You can see similar wordings as the text I quoted before. So the Defence have difficulties in understanding why this is a question for the Prosecution. Of course, it is a pleasure to inform the Prosecution of the existence of this rule, since it may be of help for witnesses called on behalf of the Prosecution, especially if they are called under Regulation No. 1 of 1994, because if the Prosecution decides not to indict any of their witnesses, of course, that goes without saying, after careful consideration and taking into account all the conditions that are set out in this Regulation, the Prosecution does not have to fear whatsoever that the Dutch government would interfere in the Prosecutor's policy. The Prosecutor requires the Defence, just for argument's sake, to give sufficient information to decide upon the request. The Defence observes, first of all, that this requirement, if we are talking about innovative, new developments of law, is entirely new. Nowhere in the existing interstate practice a party is required to give information as the Defence is asked for now. Let us just for the time being forget about the information to be given in respect of the determination that a witness is essential. Of course, it is our view that every witness that contributes to the finding of the truth should be heard, and especially witnesses that are able to testify on the whereabouts of the defendant and his activities during the rather long period in which he allegedly committed the offences are essential for the Defence anyhow. That is what I call the structural problem. But, apart from that, the Defence is not restricted to examine essential witnesses, but all witnesses that can give a statement relevant to the case. Why should we forget about this first element, the importance of the witness? Because it suggests that the Tribunal should find some balance between the importance of the statement to be expected and the seriousness of the offences the witnesses fears to be indicted for. Apart from the fact, as I said already, that this test would amount to newly invented law, it is also an impossibility. As far as witnesses 3, 7, 14 and 20 are concerned, the Defence is not aware of any misdoing of these witnesses. The Defence, of course, have no other sources than the list of indicted individuals and the statements provided to them by the Prosecutor, but we are not aware of any of these witnesses to be in danger of being indicted by the Prosecution. We have no indication whatsoever. That is what we told these witnesses, of course. But especially when there are no objective reasons for the fear to be arrested, it is even more unfair when the denial of a safe conduct would keep these witnesses off from testifying. The finding of the truth would be impaired just because of the subjective feelings of a witness and, just as the Defence has argued in respect of the withdrawal of counts 2 through 4 of the indictment, that the subjective, perhaps even temporary, feelings of a witness should not be the decisive factor for the final decision to be taken, the same is true here. Witnesses have asked us when we interviewed them whether it would be safe for them to come to The Hague, and we responded in the affirmative. We took a lot of brochures in order to inform them exactly on how things would work in this Tribunal. But then the next question came. The next question was whether Defence counsel could guarantee that they would return without any risk of being arrested or restricted in their liberty. Of course, the answer had to be no, because it is not in our power. The witnesses then often replied that they would be willing to come to The Hague if such a guarantee would be given to them. That is what the Defence now asks for, and what is given to any witness as a routine matter under circumstances where witnesses cannot be compelled to come to the site of the requesting court, that is every day's practice in the law of international assistance, mutual assistance, in criminal matters. But even if the situation was different, and if the Prosecutor was investigating the conduct of witnesses, perhaps these witnesses, or perhaps even would have indicted them already, this would be no reason to take a different position. I again refer, first of all, to the continuous State practice which, in the view of some authors, even has reached the level of customary law. I see that my pages are not -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a couple questions maybe to give you some direction because we have reviewed the motion, and let me ask you this. First of all, is there any provision in our Rules, in the Tribunal's Rules, for the granting of safe conduct? If there is not any provision, is there any language in the Statute of the Tribunal that you believe supports an inherent power on the part of the Tribunal to grant safe conduct? If I understand your request now, you want an order that would be directed, I gather, to the Prosecutor and not to in any way restrain the liberty of any of these four individuals who may come here to testify? Does that differ than the usual safe conduct rules that you have talked about in that it is an order that emanates from a country directed to another country not to interfere in the passage of the witness to the country issuing the order -- and, of course, we are not a country?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, you are not a country. First of all, the problem, as far as the Netherlands is concerned, is solved, as I told you, because there is such a safe conduct already in the agreement between the United Nations and the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not asking for an order from that in that regard. That is why I wanted to know exactly what you are asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No. So, the only problem then is that the Prosecution has powers to detain and to arrest people on Dutch territory. Of course, I am aware of the complications if would you have to enter into an agreement with, for example, Austria, Germany, well, most of the countries between -- sorry. I am aware of what kind of problems that would raise, but since modern technology, especially flying from one country to another, has taken away a lot of the importance of transit rules in international criminal law, whether it is extradition or whether it is mutual assistance. So, as a matter of fact, I would rather first concentrate on what would happen and what might be the main risk, at least the witness's fear that it is their risk, not to be arrested in Austria, but to be arrested by the Prosecutor's Office of the Tribunal. So, we do ask for an order of the court that the Prosecutor would not arrest someone or limit its liberty in whatever other way while being in The Hague perhaps even in these premises because the Prosecutor might have the right to arrest people within the premises of this Tribunal since, as you know, the Dutch government is not exercising any power on these premises. I explained to you that even if some of these witnesses would be under investigation -- they are not, as far as we know, but you will understand the decision to be taken goes, perhaps, a bit further, goes a bit beyond this case, perhaps -- the results will still be unfair for the defendant. So let us assume that the witness is relevant because he committed the offences himself or aided and abetted these offences; if he does not appear as a witness, there is a considerable risk that a decision in the case will be given on the basis of cripple information. This price is paid without any advantage for the Prosecution in the case against that witness. He was at large before and he is still at large after the trial. If a safe conduct would have been granted to him, the situation would have been exactly the same, at least for the Prosecutor, and for the witness, but not for the defendant. He is the victim of not granting a safe conduct to the witness and the Tribunal has, under these circumstances, to take a decision in the case against this defendant upon a defective basis. It is finally the quality of the administration of justice that is at stake and that is, as far as the defendant is concerned, the fairness of his trial. These, of course, are also the underlying thoughts of the widespread use of the blind granting of safe conducts in treaties, conventions and even under domestic law if it relates to the international co-operation in criminal matters. So, the Defence is not seeking any drastic relief, as the Prosecutor puts it, but would like normal standards, the normal standard of safe conduct where a witness cannot be compelled to appear, normal standards to be applied, especially where there is an indication that a lack of a safe conduct keeps the witnesses away and I think there is such an indication. I come back now to what I said before, whether there exists something like a structural exceptional situation. I am not aware of any jurisdiction that has to function in similar circumstances as this Tribunal has to do. I am not aware of any situation where the Defence is struggling with the problem that all their witnesses are in a country in which it is almost impossible to compel them to do whatever they should do. So there is these structural exceptional circumstances, apart from whether we would have to offer the proof of the existence of such a situation. That is my advantage compared to my colleague, Wladimiroff. Since there is no provision in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence nor in the Statute, I am not bound by that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I asked you. Is there? There is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You see, I have not forgotten your question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But your argument, since we are chatting about this, is there is no rule, no explicit rule, but we have our Rule 54 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence that does provide ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You can give such orders as you deem fit, yes -- the general, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- that a Judge or a Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants and transfer orders as may be necessary for the purposes of an investigation or for the preparation or conduct of the trial. It is your position, at least in your submission, that we have that inherent power -- well, we have the power to issue safe conduct orders pursuant to Rule 54 ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- and that it should be done because the Prosecutor has an internal memorandum that you referred to in your papers that allows the Prosecutor, I gather, to make an arrangement with the witness whereby the Prosecutor will agree with that witness not to prosecute the witness. So it is your position that what is good for the goose is good for the gander? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we referred to that Regulation of the Prosecutor, but I find it even more important that it is standing practice always in similar situations. So I would rather not rely just on that regulation because, first of all, it is created by the Prosecution, so I would not say that it makes bad law, but it is not immediately convincing to us that that is the right solution for the situation. So, therefore, we would rather rely upon the practice, as I told you, United States, apart from two exceptions and, of course, they have found other solutions in the treaties with Mexico and Canada, so it is not that under these treaties, you find it everywhere where justice has to be administered where the witnesses are abroad and cannot be compelled to appear. You find it everywhere in the world. As I told you, some authors even say that it reached the level of customary law. It is always done without any requirement of proving that this witness is of vital importance, or to give a court the opportunity to balance whether the consequences, just not being bothered while they are present, not for the further future, whether this should be in balance or not. No, it is a blind granting in all these treaties and in all these conventions of safe conduct. Therefore, the Defence is reluctant to offer additional information that has been requested alternatively by the Prosecutor. Perhaps for these four witnesses it might not be that much of a problem, but it would be contrary to the fundamental aspect of the concept of a safe conduct and its use in international criminal law, although, as I said for these witnesses, perhaps it would do no harm to them at all. The Defence is also aware of the far-reaching consequences for the case law of this Tribunal if we, as the Defence team of the accused, would easily admit the existence of an obligation to provide the kind of information the Prosecutor would ask for. The Defence, therefore, submits to the Trial Chamber to decide the fundamental aspects first. The Defence will then know whether there is any need for providing further information and what kind of information would be needed. Since the identity and the addresses of the witnesses concerned are known already, it might not be that difficult for the Prosecutor to find out about any investigations against these witnesses. If they would like to have the dates of birth as well, we might informally give them to them, but we would rather stick to the fundamental aspects of the question. I make one final remark: The Prosecution has said that a fair trial is good enough. It must not necessarily be a perfect trial. But I think we will have all to do our utmost best to make this trial to be fair at all under very difficult circumstances, circumstances I regard as being structural. Denying the motion as far as the safe conduct is concerned will not have the effect of downgrading the perfect trial to a fair trial, but, rather, it would involve a risk of downgrading a trial to a trial that may not be fair any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, as I understand it then, all you seek is protection while the witnesses are here in The Hague and are waiting to give evidence or are giving evidence or very shortly afterwards from arrest or indictment by the Prosecution? You do not seek any protection if we could give it, which I doubt, for interference by countries through which they may have to pass and the like?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we seek, as a matter of fact. It is a practical problem when we can get them from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina where they live directly to the Netherlands, because in the Netherlands it is no problem, if the Tribunal causes no problems, because you have seen in this Rule 18 of the Agreement that the Dutch make a reservation if they are ordered by the Tribunal -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But that Agreement is Dutch US?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, UN, United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is in the basic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I did not hear you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So there are no problems. Of course, I would like to draw your attention that a similar situation might exist also if witnesses are testifying in video link but then because you cannot compel them to come to the studio in Banja Luka, or wherever it might be. So we might have similar situations there where we cannot compel the witnesses to appear, and that is exactly what Mr. Wladimiroff asked for, that they not be arrested when they appear to testify in a Banja Luka court, in a studio, or something like that, so we have a similar situation. But we are not bothered that much at this moment about Austria and Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So this has nothing do with granting indemnity, the sort of material that is dealt with in Regulation 1, I think it is, of the Prosecutor's -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, it goes far further -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is much less. What you are seeking is very much less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What they can do with their own power without any approval of the court goes far further than we ask for, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For these four witnesses, you ask for safe conduct or video link. If you are granted video link for these four witnesses, I gather, we would not have to address the issue of safe conduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, it is our primary option to have them here in The Hague because that is where they should be but, of course, as an alternative, we seek that they will be examined by means of video link, but I draw already the attention to it that while elaborating the practical circumstances under which a video link would take place, and that is what Mr. Wladimiroff already told you, that we might have a similar problem there of risks of being arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Orie. Who will speak for the Prosecution? Are you finished, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, I think Mr. Wladimiroff wants to whisper me something. Mr. Wladimiroff draws my attention to Article 29 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence -- no, it is the Statute, yes -- Article 29 states -- it is under (2) -- "shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by the Trial Chamber including but not limited to", then it says under (D), "the arrest or detention of persons". If it is not limited to the arrest or detention of persons, you could interpret this Rule 29(2)(D) as well as saying since these witnesses are needed in The Hague, they should not be arrested abroad when they are on their way to The Hague. So it is an extensive interpretation of this Rule, but it clearly says that the orders, not just requests, but orders are not limited to. Apart from that, there is something in Article 30 about the treatment of other persons including the accused required at a seat of the International Tribunal shall be accorded such treatment as is necessary for the proper functioning of the International Tribunal. If your Trial Chamber would think it important for witnesses to come to The Hague and to testify and not be by reasons of fear to be arrested, should be encouraged to come, then perhaps these other persons might be given such treatment as is necessary for the proper functioning of the International Tribunal, and it would mean no arrest, no restriction of free movement of liberty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You also want that then in the order, not just limiting the Prosecutor, but limiting states, any states, that the witness may travel through?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is a very attractive idea to extend the safe conduct and to that extent I must admit that the Prosecutor was perfectly right that I introduced an undefined concept, but to extend it whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you want both then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do appreciate that now the Defence has defined for us what it does mean by safe conduct, it is all well and good to say many states have defined it, but of course until the Defence tells us they have adopted those definitions for their purposes we do not know what they mean. Now they have done that, we do appreciate that and find it enlightening. We would suggest, however, that the argument that the states have voluntarily agreed to bind themselves and limit themselves in their abilities does not have total relevance for our proceedings here. As we understand the safe conduct provisions in these treaties, one country and the other countries involved in the treaties each agree that, for example, if State A has a person who has committed a crime and State B wants the person, then under the safe conduct provisions, State B would agree that they would not arrest the person or hold the person for the crimes. However, State A is not prohibited from arresting that person. They can arrest them. It is the state to which they are travelling that would voluntarily agree to restrict their powers. Here in the Tribunal, of course, we are not states. We are not a state. We are not, the Office of the Prosecutor, a state which is entering into a treaty provision with the Trial Chamber. We are, in fact, a Tribunal that is international in scope but is not a sovereign entity. So there is a difference. The Defence does, in fact, seek to ask this Trial Chamber to bind nation states not to pursue their own interests, and to refrain from arresting individuals against whom they may have very strong evidence of very serious offences. Now they talk about -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not follow you at all. Are you suggesting that 3, 7, 14 and 20 are such persons because I do not follow why you are objecting to their coming here giving evidence and returning.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: In effect, you are because you are saying you will not agree to safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But if you know nothing against these four, I do not understand your attitude.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Our attitude, first of all, has to do with the entire concept of granting safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: For these four?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For anyone, the concept for anyone. There is that to deal with. Secondly, as far as these four are concerned, our question again goes back to what we put in our brief, and that is the Defence needs to make a showing. They say, do we have evidence that these people were involved in crimes? Our question is why do these people feel they will be arrested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You seem to be wasting a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But I think not. I think there is a principle involved, and that is a showing that if a person has a real fear of arrest, because if they do not have a real fear based on some real facts, what the Defence is basically asking this Trial Chamber to do is to grant what is truly a drastic measure to witnesses who may not have any need of that sort of protection. For less drastic -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Why do you say it is "drastic"?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Safe conduct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. You are not granting indemnity. You can arrest them, if you can, when they return to Yugoslavia. You can arrest them before they come.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Any measures such as this which tells us that we must limit our powers is a drastic measure and it is that context I am talking about. As far as the Trial Chamber ordering such a measure, it is even more drastic because the Trial Chamber through that order, as the Defence has indicated, would not only be limiting the Prosecutor's discretion to act upon evidence concerning crimes, but would be at least purporting to limit the right of independent states to act upon such matters. That should only be done if there has been a sufficient showing that, No. 1, there is a real fear that this person needs safe conduct, because if it is merely palliative, then this Trial Chamber is being asked to provide what is categorised as a very drastic measure with no basis, for no reason.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose my concern is that we are being asked to just grant carte blanche without knowing what it is we are being asked to grant and for whom. Of course, it is not in the Rules, but we have issued a number of orders and granted a lot of relief that is not specifically provided for in the Rules, but it just seems to me that before we do something, we need to know what it is we are being asked to do and for whom. I do not know who these people are who are coming here and who I am saying no-one will bother you, and that is my only concern. I need more information about these people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is our concern.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because I do not know who it is that is coming here. For me to tell anyone, "Do not arrest them", I do not know who they are. That is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is our concern as well. That is why it goes to why do these people fear arrest? If they say they have no reason to fear it, that is one thing; if they say: "Because I worked in this position and in this position these things happened", then you know, well, this is a person who potentially was engaged in this degree of culpability. The Defence has made reference to the Prosecutor's Regulation. That Prosecutor's Regulation involves a very careful balancing of relative culpability. That is why the Prosecution suggested that upon a showing, a proper showing, that these people are essential, that if we can only get them here through a safe conduct because they have committed such crimes that they have to have safe conduct, then perhaps the better reasoned position would be to tell the Prosecution: "This is an essential Defence witness. They are criminally culpable. If you will not agree to this, then we perhaps have to stay these proceedings", but there has been no showing to make that sort of determination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me say this about the Regulation, and then may be we should talk about it a little bit, it came about because when we were drafting the Rules, there was a suggestion by one country that we have plea bargaining. That was roundly rejected -- well, not roundly but by many of the judges it was rejected, no plea bargaining. It was rejected because at least the judges considered that the crimes at least that were listed in our subject matter jurisdiction reached the level of jus cogens, and that we did not have that power and it would be very inappropriate for us to grant that kind of plea bargaining. We determined that we would not do that. The Prosecutor has done something else on its own, and I suppose that is your business, but once again I am very concerned about what it is that I am being asked to do and for whom. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Judge Stephen, in response to your concerns, we do not want to waste this court's time, but our concern is this. You are being asked without a showing to provide certain relief. What they are basically telling you is, give these people the right to safe passage, to safe conduct, that nothing will be done to them, even though they say there is no basis for any cause to believe they are criminally involved anyway. That appears to be an order that you are going to, No. 1, have to get into what are the conditions upon which you will grant safe passage, and if your conclusion is, we will grant it where nobody is culpably involved, that kind of order, we suggest, is not something you should make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You must know, do you not, whether you have a reason to indict any one of these four?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We know, based upon what we have now, what our position is. We do not know what other evidence we may not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But at the moment you have no evidence suggesting that you might indict them?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: In that case, nothing whatever is lost by safe conduct. You are frightened you may discover between now and the time that they come some evidence?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, or the countries through which they pass may have evidence the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So an order which would be subject to an application by you to withdraw the safe conduct would be acceptable to you ---

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What we would -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: -- if you discover something?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Rather than have the court have to go into this entire issue again which we believe you would have to go into extensively because you would have to discuss the conditions under which you would grant safe conduct ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You would rather have nothing?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would rather, if the court were to order us to do anything, offer up some sort of statement to the court and the Defence as to whether at this time we have any evidence to suggest their criminal culpability; if we say we do not, then we believe that that should be all that is offered. We are just very concerned about the court getting into a position where they are ordering safe conduct in a situation where no showing has been made that, No. 1, it is even required, because it may set a meaningless exercise, but to get there you have to discuss the entire issue of safe conduct which, we suggest, is a very complicated issue and a very drastic measure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We did discuss the possibility -- we, the judges -- of encouraging the Prosecutor to just simply tell the Defence whether one of these persons is indicted now, because in the Defence's motion, they did not present it today in argument, but they say, you know, there are a number of people who have been indicted and the indictments are sealed, and they do not whether they are one of these people. Is it possible for to you tell them whether one of these four people has been indicted?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And that indictment is sealed?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Are you going to?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, your request is something we will certainly follow up. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, but here and now?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know whether you need to do it in public.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would want to check that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But if you do, it seems to me the need for safe conduct goes away, at least in so far as the Defence is concerned, that these persons have been indicted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Well, that is -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know yet whether I, as a judge, what privilege I am giving and to whom I am giving it to. That is my only concern.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is a concern, but it appears from the Defence argument that these witnesses as a palliative may want to have some safe conduct order. We object to giving something like that as a palliative to a witness. We are willing tell the Defence if these people have been indicted. We are certainly willing to do that, but we believe their request goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have been told that we must recess after an hour and 10 minutes because of the conditions that we are operating under. Mr. Orie, you have spent about 35 minutes presenting your argument. Can you wrap up quickly, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I can try to do so. First of all, I would like to ask you, your Honours, to imagine what happens with this case or any other case once the first witness that appears without a safe conduct will be arrested. You will have no witnesses any more that are living in the territory. So it will have a huge effect on the functioning of the Tribunal. Then I do not understand, as a matter of fact, that what is accepted, whether we are talking about murders, whether we are talking about people committing genocide, or whatever case, what is accepted already for decades in international criminal law without giving any reason. It is not understood as giving something to the witness, but it is always understood as you have to make up your mind; either you do not do it, you do not have a witness, that means quality of justice because poor, or you accept that the situation will still be the same as it was before, but at least that the interest of justice has been served by the appearance of the witness. So that is accepted by all countries for many, many years, for decades. I have text already from the beginning of this age and that is what is contested by the Prosecution at this moment. Then just a brief remark on whether we could bind other states. I am a bit puzzled by the reluctance of binding other states, because if you look at the 15 or 20 legislations that have entered into force now in all countries concerning the co-operation with the Tribunal, you will find that all these countries find themselves bound to do whatever the Tribunal orders them to do. I mean, if you look at this more or less -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If that were so, I mean, the Prosecutor has indicted 57 people, do you know how many arrest warrants have been executed by the world, by the non-ZIP -- I am sorry, two this morning; Bosnia-Herzegovina executed two. So it looks like we are starting to move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it is a fundamental issue because it is exactly where the Prosecutor argues that states were binding themselves on a voluntary basis to do this or not to do it. First of all, they are doing it all in all mutual assistance treaties, but apart from that, the Tribunal is the only who is in a situation that can give orders to national states. So I think we are in a lucky situation that we could do it and we are not dependent on the voluntary co-operation of third states. Again it has been argued whether there is a real fear and whether there is any reason to fear to be arrested would be part of the test to be applied. I again repeat, would it not be worse if a witness thinks that there is a reason for arrest although it is totally unfounded, would it not be even worse that this witness would not appear in this court? Apart from that, nothing is lost. We are not giving gifts to witnesses. We only let the interests of justice prevail for a very short period of time while we cannot get hold of an indicted person or an accused person anyhow, but at least the circumstance, that he is still at large, does not influence other cases. I think that is at stake. That is also the reason why it is just a routine matter in the interstate mutual assistance. If the Prosecutor asks whether it is not a drastic measure to ask them to refrain from exercising that power, I would say, first of all, all Prosecutors Offices all over the world under these conventions are restricted in the exercise of their powers and they are glad do it in the interests of justice. I think that is the most important one and most important thing, and I do not think that it would create any surprise when these kind of orders were issued to be respected by third states because all these states are used to this system.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: One sentence, your Honour. All of these determinations are based upon an adequate showing that the witness is important enough and that means what the witness will say, and that has not been made yet.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, do you have anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would say that that is exactly what is not required in the usual application of the safe conduct provisions. It is a routine matter. You are not giving away anything; you are just serving the interests of justice in this case even if it would look a bit silly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, could you provide the Tribunal with some documentation to that effect? In your motion you request safe conduct, but it was not clear, at least to me, what it is that you wanted. It is clear now what you want, and that is to ask that the Prosecutor not be required to in any way restrict the liberty of persons who come. Also, you said it would be attractive and I gather you would want then the Tribunal to issue an order precluding states from detaining a witness who we have summoned. You say that the jurisprudence, at least, under those safe conduct provisions in state agreements, agreements between states, there is no requirement that the person who receives this safe conduct make any showing that there is a need for it. If they ask for it, it is routinely given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Even if they do not ask for it, it is just a routine matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If they do not ask for it, but can you give us some support for that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will be glad to do so. I remember that last time ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you do it by Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I could do it by Monday, but if you require me again to have it all in English by that time, it was -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What countries?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have literature -- of course, I have English literature -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The United States?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The United States.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Australia, that is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least the treaty provisions. I could give you a lot of treaty provisions, if you would like to have them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you will give us the United States and the Australia, you pointed to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Dutch Australian, yes, the Dutch Australian treaty. I have, as a matter of fact, a legal text in Dutch written by a Dutch author who explains very precisely, has written a book on witness abroad testifying in another country, and he is spending some four, five or six pages to the issue of safe conduct. At least I could provide you with something next Monday. I will do my utmost best to make it as complete as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before 5.00 then provide us with that information, provide the Prosecutor with a copy of that. If the Prosecutor wishes to respond, then will you do it -- we are starting trial on Tuesday for sure at 10 a.m. -- at some point before the close of that day, on 7th? Very good. That then concludes the argument. There are more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have one question. Are you not labouring under some self-denying ordinance, because you have, in fact, given statements in relation to each one of these four, saying that they are police officers, or were, in Prijedor and saying also their evidence is vital, yet you seem to be saying: "We do not need to saying anything"; maybe you do not, but you have already said that, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that we gave a general picture of the importance -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You said those two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we also asked for summoning them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We asked to summon them as well. I think the relevance of the witness might be more important for summoning them ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- than for granting -- so for that reason we gave that information. But if, for example, for another witness we would have given no information at all, and you would say: "OK, we will summon them anyhow", we feel there is no need for giving additional information for granting them a safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You seem to be standing on principle unnecessarily because you have given information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well .....

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the context of a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor says that this is not the kind of information you would need to take a decision on that. So, to that extent, I have not given the information to the Prosecution, but we have given some information on these witnesses, that is true.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At some point I think we will have to end this discussion on this one motion. We will stand in recess, please, for 10 minutes and we will return and then we will hear a few questions that we wish to pose regarding the Prosecutor's motion to compel statements of the Defence. Then we will talk about the requests that both parties have made for the Trial Chamber to address issues in the pretrial briefs and then some miscellaneous matters that we need to resolve before we begin the trial on Tuesday. We will stand in recess for 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has filed a motion to compel witness statements from the Defence. I had a couple of questions. It is just not clear from the papers that we have, from the many status conferences that we have had, what has happened when the parties. First of all, was there an agreement by Mr. Wladimiroff to provide the Prosecutor with statements of witnesses? If there was such an agreement, did those statements relate to witnesses who were alibi witnesses and/or expert witnesses or did that agreement go beyond either their alibi or expert witnesses? That is the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I first address -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just finish the questions. The second question was whether or not the names of all witnesses that both parties intend on calling have been exchanged. I was under the assumptions that the names of all witnesses had been exchanged and, of course, we received last night, I believe, a letter from the Defence saying that that was not the case. So, please if you can address that, Mr. Wladimiroff? You can if you wish first even though it is the Prosecutor's motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would just make some observation about the issue of there being an agreement or not and then Stephen Kay will deal with the motion as such. It has been discussed with the Prosecution Office lots of times, and last in the month of, let us say, June up to September/October last year, the Defence took the position that we had to consider to give them what we were collecting. It is true that I have expressed the consideration on my part that it was something we had to decide, though we did not decide it and we did certainly not agree on it. So we have shared our opinions about it, our feelings about it, with the Prosecution. There is no doubt about it. I maintain that they were under the impression that we may proceed to a decision to do so. But, after consideration by the end of 1995, after we went further with our witnesses, it became clear there was no obligation under the Rules and there was no need to do so. Further, after we learned much more about the fears of the witnesses, we decided it would be highly inappropriate to do so because most witnesses asked us not to reveal any of their interview information to the Prosecution, and under the Rules we felt we had no obligation and, therefore, we could guarantee them that we would not. So, in my opinion, there was no agreement. We shared our considerations but no agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, I confirm what my friend has said, but I think there was a misunderstanding. Certainly on our part, we were under the impression that this material was definitely going to be handed over. But I agree that the Defence did not specifically say: "We agree at a certain point in time we are going to this". It was discussed on the basis, as Mr. Wladimiroff has put it, I think he used the terms from memory, "I know we have an obligation to do this", or something to that effect, and that is why we went along and we assumed that was going to occur. Your Honour raised the other issue about exchange of names. Certain lists of witnesses have been provided to us, list of names have been provided to us. What we are not aware of is whether or not these names at the end of the day will amount to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, do you view that there was an agreement to exchange statements for any of the witnesses? This came from a status conference, I believe, that Judge Stephen conducted -- I do not want to get into too much detail because it was conducted in camera -- on February 13th of this year. You have the transcript, and if you have the transcript, Mr. Wladimiroff, you can look at it and see just what was said. I was not there so I do not know, except to look at the transcript. But is it your understanding that there was an agreement to exchange statements -- an agreement on the part of the Defence to provide you with any statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We were under that impression that they were going to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Statements for what now? Alibi witnesses, all witnesses, expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We were under the impression it was all witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Has the Defence provided the Prosecutor with the names of its witnesses other than alibi witnesses and expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A list of names have been provided to the Prosecution some time ago in relation to a request by the Defence for assistance in the location of witnesses. Whether those names will, at the end of the day, mean that they are witnesses or not, we, the Prosecution, do not know, except that we have been given a list of names. We do not know whether they are exhaustive. We do not whether they are merely for investigative purposes by the Defence. It was really in conjunction with a request for assistance by us in locating people.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So the only names you know of, the only list you know of, would be the alibi witnesses and, of course, the expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you want to speak to what this agreement was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that is the position. I think if one looks at what took place, it may be it can be read as being a misunderstanding between those parties.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not have a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think that was before you joined officially as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is the foot of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It does not state precisely that it is the revelation of the contents of statements. It refers to an obligation in relation to the matter. We are well provided with the statements by the Prosecution. We do not, in fact, have all the statements from the Prosecution. There are still some witnesses in respect of whom statements have not been taken. Other statements that we have been provided with recently complete the picture more fully, but there have been a number who have been provided to us in the form of a short form proof of what it is anticipated they might talk about. In relation to the text here, Mr. Wladimiroff speaking in English refers to an obligation. He does not feel that we are yet in a position to comply, although we have provided the Prosecution with a list of names, not with the statements of them because not all of them have been interviewed. It refers to a list of names of potential witnesses which Mr. Niemann has most recently been referring to. The names disclosed by us officially as witnesses are those on our alibi notice. As a result of a recent trip to Bosnia by Miss de Bertodano, we have supplemented that list with a further eight alibi witnesses. So it amounts to some 36 alibi witnesses that have been disclosed by name and address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has a supplement been filed with the court as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was filed today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A lot of things have been today -- good things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They are now 36?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are now 36 alibi witnesses. I think the court appreciates the difficulty we have had in relation to collection of material, problems we have had with investigators and we have had to take the matter completely and fully in our hands in relation to this matter by the present Defence team. We have made far better progress than previous arrangements really afforded us. In relation to this matter, I do not think we can ever underestimate quite the difficulties that one goes through in taking these statements from witnesses out there. Earlier material was very incomplete and unprofessionally done (although by apparent professionals) and completely inadequate for a trial of this nature. When one meets a potential witness, it is not a question of just sitting down with a tape recorder and conducting an interview; you have to spend quite a bit of time explaining why you are there, what the consequences are, that they can trust you in speaking to you, that you are, in fact, a Defence attorney instructed by Mr. Tadic, and you have to build up a relationship with that particular person sufficient to get them to talk to you about matters with which you feel they can help. That often requires that you tell them that this is for the Defence, it is not for the Prosecution, and that this material will not be disclosed to the Prosecution when they talk to you, because you do not know at that stage what they are going to talk to you about, or whether they have anything relevant to tell you that will be of use in the course of the trial and the adduction of evidence. So, in those circumstances, a large number of witnesses have been told that they will be spoken to in confidence and what they have told us will be kept by us, and that when they come and their opportunity either in The Hague or Banja Luka to give evidence arises and they tell the court what took place, that is the opportunity for them to give their testimony. We do rather firmly rely on our privilege in relation to this matter, our legal professional privilege, in the circumstances in which these statements were taken. I have put in my response to the motion the circumstances that often apply. You are getting someone speaking in Serbo-Croat to a Dutch Serbian interpreter relayed to a Dutch lawyer translated into English, as happened on a number of occasions when I was out there or, in Miss de Bertodano's case, using a Dutch Serbo-Croat interpreter with an imperfect command of English then relaying it to her. We have to make our judgment in relation to the material that we are given, whether it is accurate, whether we are going to rely on it, and whether we are going to call these people. But for us to disclose the original nature of the interview with these people, we feel is extending the powers of the investigator and the Prosecution directly into our work product and our work material that is otherwise privileged. We have our alibi witnesses named. They can go and interview them, if they want. But we have no obligation, as we see it, to provide that material to them. It is their duty to investigate the case, they are bringing the allegations against us. We see it as no part of our function to be there as a cipher to provide our information and work product to them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do have, Mr. Kay, a Rule, Rule 70, that covers matter not subject to disclosure that was designed to be, essentially, a work product rule. In your response to the motion to compel, you do not refer at all to that. You simply say "a legal privilege"; at one point you say "a privilege". If you referring to Rule 70, of course, then those would be matters not subject to disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But your decision is generally that there is no rule requiring disclosure of statements, period, by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour, for the reasons set out in our response to the motion. What we are concerned with is that we are then in a position of providing material that assists the Prosecution which is not our function, and that the responsibility and the presentation of the case and its investigation is their function. It is not a question of surprise or anything like that. Those witnesses that we are obliged to supply, they can go and interview them in Prijedor and Banja Luka and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there someone from the Prosecution who would like to speak to this motion? In the interests of time, I did not want to have a long discussion about it. Actually, there were just these questions that we had. We have read very thoroughly the motion filed by the Prosecutor as well as the response from the Defence, but go ahead Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I will be very brief. Your Honours, with relation to the question, we are not suggesting that the Defence are under any obligation pursuant to the Rules as such. We are saying our motion is purely based on the fact that we would submit that the orderly conduct of the trial would be greatly assisted if the Prosecution had some advance notice of what these witnesses were about to attest to prior to them doing it; I think we have suggested 30 days, but a period prior to them giving evidence. We submit that that would assist in the orderly conduct of the trial. If your Honours were with us in that, we submit that such an order would be made under Rule 54. We submit that it is not a question of saying that the Defence has an obligation and that we are arguing that they must comply. We are submitting that this would assist the orderly conduct. The only other matter is if there are circumstances in which the taking of the statements created all sorts of problems, as has been suggested by my friend, we are not necessarily asking for their materials that were taken at the relevant time. We are merely asking for proof or some sort of indication of what these witnesses will attest to when they give their evidence, if that assists your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rule 54, what would we have done without Rule 54? It has been cited and it is always cited. Whenever a party wants something that is not specifically in the Rules, they refer to Rule 54, and I am very happy that is in there. You have asked, though, for 30 days in advance. If the Defence was to turn over the witness statements after the witness testified, would that be assisting the Prosecution in proving their case, Mr. Kay? If you look at Article 21 of the Statute, the burden of proof, or would it in any way violate any self-incrimination privilege?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It does; it strikes at the heart, as I put it in my response to the motion, of the role of the Defence team in this case. As one can see where confusion or misinterpretation may have arisen, a court could find itself in the dangerous position of advocate then being impeached or a disagreement over the reliability of the record taken by the advocate. For these very good reasons, this is an area where courts traditionally try not to enter recognising that the good orderly conduct of the trial often requires that kind of embargo to be placed in relation to the preparation of Defence materials. That is clearly accepted by most jurisdictions. We do not see why we should give statements after one of our witnesses has given evidence from our own resources. That is our material. We are not bringing the charges. The Prosecution are bringing the charges and, out of necessity, must disclose their statements so that we can either plead guilty or not guilty, so that we can find out where it was that we were alleged to have been at the time a crime is alleged to have been committed and file an alibi notice and respond to the allegations within the indictment. Our function is not like that in this case. If a witness has told us something and we call that witness, our materials, we say, remain with us. If our witness goes off proof and refers to matters that they did not originally tell us about, or describe matters differently, we take that risk in relation to witnesses. We cannot control them in relation to that. It would be very unusual for a Defence to start turning a witness hostile by introducing the previous testimony. Certainly in my experience of 20 years, I have never done that defending; you might do it prosecuting, as I have on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except in the United States, of course, there are Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 26.2 does require disclosure of witness statements by Defence after they testify. As a practical matter, most courts require that they be given earlier, and the Prosecutor is also under Jenks(?) Act required to give over statements after the witness testifies but, as a practical matter, it is done before. So some jurisdictions handle it differently. What you are saying, it is a legal privilege and it might fit within our Rule 70. If it is work product, then I wonder about the Prosecutor's statements? Would that be work product in that it would be their legal opinions and theories of the case or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, their opinions and theories about the case would not be disclosed to us. I think there is a danger in this matter being presented on the case: "Well, they do it, so should you". It does not really work like that, because our functions and roles are very different in relation to the trial itself. If we had known, if Professor Wladimiroff had known 18 months ago when he was stalking the highways of Prijedor taking statements in farmhouses and meeting people, he may well have gone about his business very, very differently. If I had known when I went out there and took statements in circumstances where we were forced to because there were no other ways of getting this case ready by May 7th, I would not have told witnesses that I met that this was not going to be given to the Prosecution, that "you are talking to me in confidence and you can trust me". An order being made in relation to this material now would be viewed by a number of our witnesses as a complete and utter breach of trust and our credibility in relation to the matter would be severely damaged. I cannot emphasise this enough, the process we have to go through to get statements and to show that we are not spies, we are not really prosecutors dressed up as defence attorneys and that we are independent representing the interests of the defendant. It is a process that is exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I remember reading some time ago of a proposal in England for the Defence to furnish Defence statements to the Prosecution. Has that proposal been implemented?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, the Royal Commission on Criminal Justice which reported in July 1993 made a recommendation that the Defence should disclose generally the issues in the case, so that when you went to trial you said "the issue is self-defence", and you ticked a box was the way they wanted to do it. Most people who prosecuted did not think it was necessary, as if you could not spot what the defence was going to be you should not really be doing that job. Other issues such as duress should be explained and put before the court. Under the Criminal Investigations and Procedures Bill currently going through the House of Commons at the moment, the first part of the Bill is a codification of the rules of disclosure by the Prosecution and disclosure by the Defence. Again it is not statements; it is general issues relating to how the Defence is put. It is a Bill of much controversy because there is no obligation for the Prosecution to do the same, and severe criticism about the matter by Her Majesty's judges, in particular, but there is no obligation to release Defence witness statements. It is seen as legal, professional privilege and not to be interfered with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A remark was made here which might assist the court. When you are getting this information -- I was writing it down in English, Mr. Wladimiroff would have been writing it down in Dutch -- there is no way that you then turn it to the witness and ask him to read it through and sign it, and you do not have the time and circumstances for the interpreter to go through the whole thing again and recount what you have written down. You have to get back to the hotel or whatever and put it on a dictaphone, or you have to wait until you get back to the office when you return and pool all your notes and give your impression of what the witness said. As I said, we take a grave risk in making mistakes about this because there is a language problem. But, other than a few statements taken by one of the lawyers originally on the case, Mr. Simic, who was a local lawyer in Banja Luka, who did sign a couple of statements or had them signed, they are about six line statements of little worth to anyone, particularly when you consider the case we are dealing with. Our statements are very full and often a number of pages but not signed because we do not have that kind of facility and resources. When one looks at the Prosecution statements, you see that they have been translated, they have a translator there, two investigators, they are read back, there is a declaration as to the truth and the accurate translation. We have nothing like that. This is where the simple guise of it being, "Well, we do it, so should they", it is a resource problem as well as a matter of privilege and burden of proof. We do not have that kind of facility nor circumstance to take statements in that way. To be frank, the lack of signature and lack of attestification as to the truth by the witnesses at the time, really make what is sought to be used of them as a vessel for impeachment rather unsound and probably not helpful to the court, because there will be enormous arguments over what was really said by whom to whom and through whom. Sometimes it goes through people to you. Those are my submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Very briefly, your Honours, the whole notion of this is not a totally novel issue with regard to the Rules. I am just briefly mentioning that Rule 67 (C) in certain circumstances contemplates that, so it is not as though it is totally novel. That is all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the problem that we have is that we have Rules and, of course, there are some rules not explicit. I go back to Rule 54. We have also heard with respect to two motions safe conduct discussions. Now this is perhaps the first trial. There were certain circumstances under which the Defence is operating and we will do our best to put all of these things together and reach an appropriate decision, if not today, certainly by Monday as to this motion. Now the next order of business, I think, relates to the pretrial briefs that were filed by the parties. This was a matter that was mentioned in our closed session, and that is that the Prosecutor has filed a pretrial brief, the Defence has filed a response and the Prosecutor has filed a reply. The judges asked for these briefs and we asked that you, among other things, identify your positions regarding elements of the offence and we have received those. Mr. Wladimiroff, we received a letter from you, I guess, last night saying that you wish to have matters regarding the briefs resolved before opening statements are heard and relevant decisions before the start of trial. The Prosecutor also asked for an opportunity to have resolved the various issues dealing with elements, and the sentencing evidence, before offering evidence in their case in chief. As I indicated then during the closed session we had identified four issues that we thought, or four matters, that were addressed in the pretrial briefs that perhaps you needed some direction, that is some position on the part of the Trial Chamber before you began your evidence. We wanted to tell you what our position was on those four issues, and then receive from you any other requests and see where we are. The first issue related to sentencing information. As I understand it, the position of the Prosecutor and the brief is that it should be able to offer evidence or material relating to sentencing during their case in chief from witnesses who will also testify as to the guilt of the accused. It is the position of the Defence that, no, that should be handled in a separate proceeding and there should not be allowed any testimony by a witness who is testifying as to guilt about appropriate sentence. Is that correct? Is that an accurate statement generally of your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is our position, if this will help you and I think it is important, that no information that relates exclusively to sentencing should be presented by a witness during the trial as to the guilt or the innocence of the accused. So, if a witness is testifying about guilt or in a sense of the accused, that witness should not be able at the same time to offer evidence exclusively as to sentencing. Does that help you? Does that answer at least the division, the difference of opinion? If not tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It will be of great help, your Honour, although I might have to think over the word "exclusively" for the weekend because that is what is going to be the problem I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is the problem, Mr. Orie, you are very right, because we recognise that we were asking for perhaps some trouble, and there very well may be some objection on the part of the Defence saying, no, and we will have to resolve that when it happens. At least you understand our position. The second point was whether the Trial Chamber should, if the evidence supports, find the accused guilty of a crime that is not charged in the indictment. The Prosecutor took the position that that is permitted and cited some jurisdictions from Spain, China, a number of jurisdictions, saying that even though you do not specifically charge an accused with a particular crime, if the evidence supported it and that the accused was put on fair notice of this that he was being charged, even though it was not specific, that we could find the accused guilty of that charge. The Defence said, as I recall in the brief, no, that is not so. We have reviewed the briefs and discussed this matter, and we consider, as far as our Trial Chamber is concerned, that it would not be appropriate and we will not find the accused guilty of any crime unless it is specifically charged in the indictment. Does that satisfy that issue or do you need clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am, that is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Then the next issue related to whether or not it was necessary to offer evidence as to the character of the conflict. The Defence took the position that the Appeals Chamber had found in its decision on jurisdiction that the conflict was totally internal. The Prosecutor took the position that the Appeals Chamber had found, I think, that it was international, although at some point you say that it was confusing. I agree with you that at some point, with all due respect, it is a little confusing. Under those circumstances the Trial Chamber would like to hear evidence as to the character of the conflict. In the Prosecutor's brief I believe you stated you would offer evidence as to the continuing presence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia after May 1992. So it seems to me you are ready to present the kind of evidence that we are interested in in trying to determine the applicability really of Article 2, the Grave Breaches section. Does that satisfy that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is clear for us, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the last one we thought would be appropriate was whether evidence need be offered that the crimes charged in the indictment were committed in the context of an armed conflict. The Prosecutor took the position that the Appeals Chamber had made a determination that the crimes charged in the indictment were, in fact, committed in the context. The Defence took the position that if they did it was preliminary, and that you should not be foreclosed and that the Prosecutor still has the burden of showing that these crimes that are alleged to have been committed were committed in the context of an armed conflict. We agree with the Defence, that to the extent that there was mention made of it in the Appeals Chamber's decision, evidence must be offered by the Prosecutor to show that the crimes were committed in the context of an armed conflict. Of course, as to the applicability of Article 2 or Article 3, then the nature of the conflict and the status of protective persons would have to be dealt. Are there other issues from the Prosecutor that were raised by your pretrial brief that you feel must be addressed by the Trial Chamber before you begin trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We would again ask the Trial Chamber to consider the general issue of the elements of the offences. It is the submission of this Office that in no jurisdiction does the prosecution ever enter a trial without knowing exactly what it must prove to satisfy the legal requirements of a particular crime. That knowledge, of course, is generally derived from either a legislative code or judicial precedents which are well-founded. Here, of course, we do not have the benefit of either a specific legislative code or the case law which so accurately defines the crimes as to lay out, if you will, the elements. Accordingly, we believe that in this instance this Chamber must make that decision which is why we believe in fact the Chamber requested our position on the elements and why we were so keen to provide those. We provided them at least with the impression that such a decision would be taken, so that prior to the submission of any evidence we would understand exactly what the legal requirements would be in the eyes of the Chamber for the particular crimes. I think also it is a matter for the Defence so that they understand exactly what it is they must offend against. Therefore, both parties I believe would request that you reconsider that decision about issuing a determination prior to the start of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to point out a few issues that are, in the view of the Defence, in need of being decided upon. I would first remind you that we expressed not only our views on what would be the elements of the offences, but also that we had some concern as to the specificity of the charges themselves. The Defence would very much like you to decide whether it is good enough if the Prosecutor says that victims are protected persons under one of the four Geneva Conventions, giving us not very much guidance on whether there is any violation of the grave breaches under the Fourth convention or under the Third. I just noticed that you said there cannot be alternative findings away from the charges. Well, the Defence still does not know whether the grave breaches are charges brought under the First, the Second, the Third or the Fourth Geneva Conventions. So that is still a matter of concern to the Defence. Apart from that, we have seen in the pretrial brief that a lot of definitions were given and elements were specified, although these offences have not been charged as such, but are part of the persecution charge. So that is still puzzling the Defence very much.
